member of the commission. − madam president, as commissioner oettinger unfortunately cannot be here tonight, i would like, on behalf of the commission, to welcome the carbon capture and storage (ccs) report from parliament. as we just heard from the rapporteur, a combination of technologies is needed to decarbonise europe, including renewable energy, greater energy efficiency and ccs. ccs combined with renewable energy has the potential to deliver larger emissions reductions than renewable energy alone. following the commission consultative communication on the future of ccs in europe, the role of ccs for power generation and energy-intensive industries will be addressed in the communication on the 2030 energy and climate policy framework that the commission intends to adopt next week. in the long term, support for ccs should be derived mainly from an adequate co2 price signal. further analysis of possible interim support measures needs to be undertaken. we share parliament’s view that it is essential, in parallel, to develop and successfully operate a range of full-chain demonstration projects that would help identify the most cost-efficient technologies. i agree very much with what mr davis just said: what we need to do first in europe is to gather positive experiences from a range of technologies in this field. we need the demonstration projects. they are a critical step towards ensuring the timely deployment of this technology and validating its cost-effectiveness as a climate-friendly technology. funding under the european energy programme for recovery has already supported efforts in this direction. one additional ccs project is also being assessed for co-financing under the ner300 scheme. it should be no secret to anybody, however – and it was implied in what mr davis just said – that we need more interest on the part of member states. we cannot do this without co-financing and co-interest from member states. the commission is very keen to work with the member states on gaining experience in this technology. furthermore, as was also recognised by parliament’s report, the importance of member states’ developing national low-carbon strategies and roadmaps – taking ccs into account where relevant – was highlighted as a possible support measure by some contributions to the ccs consultation launched last year. the commission welcomes the call in parliament’s report for the development of adequate co2 transport and storage infrastructure. the horizon 2020 work programme for 2014 and 2015, which includes co2 storage projects as a priority, and the connecting europe facility, for cross-border transport solutions, could support initiatives in these areas – for instance, in the north sea. here again, member state interest is a prerequisite. we share parliament’s call for closer cooperation with ccs projects worldwide. cooperation is already happening with the us, with canada and with australia. the commission attaches high importance to the proper and consistent implementation of the ccs regulatory framework across europe, with a view to supporting the demonstration and subsequent deployment of ccs in an environmentally-safe way and to enhancing public confidence in this technology. the commission notes parliament’s call for a revision of the ccs directive, particularly in relation to co2 storage liabilities. the review of the directive will start this year. we envisage that it will be a thorough exercise with broad engagement by all relevant stakeholders. the review will aim to assess the effectiveness of the directive’s provisions against the state of play of ccs in europe and its future deployment prospects. we note parliament’s insistence that it is no longer acceptable to invest in fossil-fuel-based power plants or industrial installations without proper regard for how this will be reduced in the future. i would like to reassure the members of parliament that, as part of the review of the ccs directive, due consideration will be given to the assessment of capture and storage readiness provisions. the commission welcomes the suggestions that parliament has put forward in its report as an important contribution to the ongoing debate on the best way to support the development of ccs in europe. let me finish by thanking the rapporteur and all the members of parliament involved for their work and their constructive dialogue on this. i would reiterate, however, that member states need to engage further if this is not to be only a theoretical debate but actually one of the technologies on which europe could take the lead.

parliament informed of future progress. concerning labelling the origin of meat, many initiatives are planned in the context of the new legislation on food information to consumers. these include (to complete the mandatory labelling of the origin of beef) a new regulation which has just been adopted by the commission to specify the modalities for mandatory labelling of the origin of pig, sheep, goat and poultry meat. as regards labelling the origin of meat used as an ingredient, a report opening the debate was adopted on 17 december 2013. but while such initiatives might satisfy the demands for the labelling of origin, we must recognise that such measures cannot be considered a tool to prevent fraudulent practices. the horsemeat scandal could still have arisen even if origin labelling had been mandatory at that time for the foods in question. concerning cloning, on 18 december 2013 the commission adopted two legislative proposals addressing animal welfare and ethical concerns relating to the use of the cloning technique. the first proposed directive would ban the use of the cloning technique in the european union for farmed animals and would ban imports into the european union of cloned animals. the second would ban food such as meat or milk from cloned animals from being placed on the european unionʼs market.

in writing. food safety and the protection of consumers' health have always been a key concern of the european union, which has a comprehensive and highly advanced legislative framework in these areas. however, these aspects have been joined by the related issue of food fraud, which has received increasing attention following serious scandals and cases of fraudulent labelling and other food fraud which, in addition to posing serious threats to the health of citizens, have had a serious and far-reaching impact on the eu food chain. the need for better regulation of food fraud at european level, and in particular of its scale, the factors contributing to its occurrence and possible solutions, has thus become clear, in order to protect a sector which, with its 48 million jobs and a value of eur 715 billion per year, is one of the main sectors of the eu economy. the interest is to ensure better and more complete protection of the public health of european citizens and their freedom of choice in the field of food.
in writing. food safety has always been a priority in the european union's policies. in recent years, the phenomenon of food fraud has received increasing attention following cases of fraudulent food labelling and other food fraud affecting the food chain in the european union. these cases of food fraud have had a negative impact on consumer confidence by creating a paradox: food is safer than ever, but consumer confidence is low. the main problem is that the european union does not have a generally accepted definition of food fraud, as the current european legislative framework is largely focused on food safety; the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to provide for the possibility of a national court to impose a fine on the person concerned for the infringement of the provisions of the directive. it is therefore a matter of priority to arrive at a clear and harmonised definition of food fraud at european level. i also believe that the role of the food and veterinary office in detecting food fraud should be strengthened, as should its resources. finally, cooperation between member states in crossborder investigations should be strengthened through the involvement of europol.

the next item is the report by phil bennion, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on financial participation of employees in companies’ proceeds (2013/2127(ini)) (a7-0465/2013).
member of the commission. − mr president, on behalf of the commission, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr phil bennion, the committee on employment and social affairs and the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, and the european parliament as a whole, for the work done on the report and the resolution on employee financial participation. the resolution provides a comprehensive overview of concrete initiatives which should be considered by the member states and by the commission to encourage and facilitate employee financial participation across the european union. more than 30 years of research support the conclusion that companies that are partly, or entirely, owned by their employees are more profitable, create more jobs and pay more taxes than their competitors without employee share ownership. employee share ownership also strengthens corporate governance and has a positive impact on employee motivation and also on retention. also, companies with employee share ownership do not relocate as easily as some other companies do. on the contrary, companies partially owned by employees are more strongly embedded in local communities and regions. furthermore, since employees are long-term stakeholders par excellence, broadening employee shareholding is also a source of long-term financing which can help to stabilise capital markets. the resolution also rightly emphasises the particular importance of employee share ownership for small and medium-sized enterprises. smes constitute the vital texture of our economy, and employee share ownership can help sustain the success of commercial and social enterprises. for all these reasons i welcome this resolution as an important contribution to the execution of the commission’s inclusive growth strategy to ensure that we emerge faster and stronger from the economic and financial crisis. the commission takes note of all the recommendations in the resolution, which comes at a very timely moment indeed. the commission is now implementing a pilot project on the promotion of employee ownership and participation. the purpose of this project is, firstly, to identify the reasons underpinning the wide divergences in approaches across member states. we will focus on the main drivers behind the cost and administrative complexities that are hampering a large-scale introduction of financial participation schemes, in particular in cross-border scenarios. secondly, we will analyse in detail the possible regulatory and non-regulatory actions that might be proposed or undertaken by the commission. it goes without saying that we will consider parliament’s recommendations very carefully.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place on tuesday, 14 january 2014.

president of the commission. − mr president, madam president-in- office, honourable members, with the conclusion of the lithuanian presidency, the european union ended the year 2013 on a high note. the successful closure of ireland’s support programme proves that, when adjustment and assistance go hand in hand, we can overcome even the most serious kinds of crisis in a eurozone country. spain’s exit from its specific banking programme shows that we can effectively address grave concerns about the financial institutions, even in a larger economy. it proves that, through reform and increased responsibility, we can put the banking sector on a sound footing once again. with the accession of latvia, the eurozone is expanding – another unambiguous sign of renewed confidence in the euro. these are encouraging signs for the european union and especially for member states that still face hard times and challenging transitions. i believe that europe as a whole should take heart that the situation can be, and is being, turned around. it is hugely important to note that, at the start of this new year – a crucial year for europe – we are in a far better place than we were at any time since the start of the financial crisis. we owe this only to combined, concerted and continued efforts at national and european level. honourable members, i want to pay a sincere tribute to the lithuanian presidency. through a lot of hard work and commitment, the lithuanian team has been able to push forward a number of delicate and decisive initiatives. for the months ahead, our top priority remains the banking union. over the past five years, we have undertaken a fundamental reform of the way banks are regulated and supervised. we want a thriving and responsible european banking sector, at the service of the real economy, where banks – not taxpayers – carry the costs of their own mistakes. today, europe’s banks are better capitalised, better regulated to manage risks, and better supervised. we are now at the beginning of the end of public bank bail-outs, with the welcome agreements reached by the co-legislators in december on the bank resolution directive and deposit guarantee schemes. banking union is a crucial sign of our commitment to a genuine and deep economic and monetary union and to restoring decent lending conditions throughout the euro area, and it is an essential part of decoupling bank risks from sovereign debt. so it is now imperative to work for agreement on the single resolution mechanism, which is the last building block needed for a genuine european banking union. the council set out its position in december, opening the door for negotiations with parliament. as you know, the commission would have preferred a system based fully on the community approach. the commission has rigorously defended an article 114 legal base for its proposal. like parliament, we are concerned that the introduction of an intergovernmental dimension to addressing the transfer and mutualisation of funds will undoubtedly add further unnecessary complexity. but at the same time – and we have to face reality – there appears to be no other approach which will obtain the necessary support in council. so the question is not whether we are happy with the council position. the question is rather whether we can afford to waste the opportunity to reach a final agreement before the end of this parliamentary term. can we afford to put at risk the emerging signs of returning confidence? this is what is at stake. so i believe we should now work hand in hand as parliament and commission to achieve our goal of a single resolution mechanism, which is the indispensable final piece of a european banking union. for that, we need to fight to the limit to ensure that the intergovernmental dimension is kept to the absolute minimum of what is politically necessary. we should also be very vigilant in making sure the outcome remains fully compatible with, and upholds the primacy of, eu law. 2013 was also very much the year in which we proved the maturity and the effectiveness of the economic governance framework as we have developed it since the start of the crisis, including the tools of the ʻtwo pack’ implemented for the first time. this european semester cycle offered less drama than previous editions but more genuine debate and, in the end, more gratifying decisions. we can build on these experiences and the policy results when we further focus on growth and jobs in the months to come. we have at the same time continued to deepen the debate about the future of our governance framework, notably at the december summit, with a real in-depth discussion about contractual arrangements that could expand the partnership between member states and the european union, deepen the effective solidarity between countries and reinforce the sense of ownership of reforms within member states. this must certainly include paying more attention to the social dimension of economic and monetary union, which is the topic of a communication from the european commission and of two ministerial debates under the lithuanian presidency. as part of the european semester, we have proposed a new scoreboard to allow for better and earlier identification of major social and employment problems. from the beginning, this has been an integral part of what our reform efforts are all about. there is now broad support across europe to fine-tune our approach further, to focus our attention even more and to work more closely with the social partners in order to improve results. earlier in the lithuanian presidency we reached an agreement that forms the very basis of the european union’s role and ability to make sure reforms lead to more jobs and better opportunities: the multiannual financial framework. i remember well the extensive discussions we had, between the council and parliament, and also how we were together able to make the final deal. i want once again to thank all the leaders in the european parliament who worked with us to conclude that historic agreement. as i have always stated, our response to the crisis has to go beyond fiscal consolidation and structural reform. they are indispensable, to be sure, but we also need investment, and for many of our regions the european budget is the first – and even in some cases almost the only – source of public investment. so it is vital that we make progress and do not delay its implementation. one aspect remains especially urgent, and it is one in which european institutions and actors have strongly taken the lead but where cooperation with member state governments is essential: youth unemployment. the commission has been giving top priority to all initiatives aimed at tackling youth unemployment, but implementation by the member states remains crucial. by 31 december 2013, 17 out of 20 member states in which the youth unemployment rate is above 25 %, and which are therefore eligible to benefit from the youth employment initiative, had submitted their youth guarantee implementation plans, so three member states are still missing. an important contribution to fostering action on the ground was the agreement reached on the european social fund regulation, and in particular on the youth employment initiative. now that the framework for the youth employment initiative is set, it is crucial that national authorities proceed with speedy programming of activities in order to ensure quick and effective implementation. also, to further link up europeans with job opportunities across the european union, the commission will later this week present the way we aim to strengthen the eures network. i call on all member states and social partners not to slow down this issue, which is so decisive for our credibility and for the future of our young people. also regarding the social agenda, let us not forget that we successfully concluded on the posting of workers issue under the lithuanian presidency as well. this was a very important agreement and an important step towards encouraging people to use their right of free movement, and to do so in a way which is – and is seen to be – socially fair. honourable members, the lithuanian presidency gave priority to the vilnius summit so that we could move forward with the eastern partnership. indeed, it was a very important and, i would say, historic summit, and we were able to make progress in our relationship with our eastern partners, especially by moving towards economic integration and political association with those who are ready and willing for it. it also confirmed how challenging the situation in ukraine is, and why we should not give up on our commitment to those countries in our neighbourhood that want to link up with the freedoms and the way of life they see in the european union. indeed, one of the most important moments of the vilnius summit was on the streets of kiev. the summit was not only in vilnius; it was also on the streets of kiev. we saw europe at its most popular: a beacon of hope and values and a guarantee of human rights and liberties. around diplomatic tables, we saw europe at its best: united in defending ukrainian citizens’ dignity and opinions and ready to support their sovereign right to decide on their own destiny and to improve their chances of a better, more prosperous and more democratic future. at a time when we have so many people disappointed in the european union, i think that to see young people – and sometimes not so young people – in the freezing kiev nights, holding so high the flags of the european union, confirms how important the european union and its values are, not only for us here in our member states, but also for the rest of the world. other elements of the eastern partnership were also pursued. the european union-georgia association agreement was initialled, and so was the association agreement with moldova. visa facilitation was on the table, and the joint declaration of the vilnius summit made clear that we will enhance cooperation in strategic areas in the future as well. the tragic events of lampedusa – i had the occasion to witness the dramatic consequences personally on that island – and the unforgettable deaths of 350 people signalled and symbolised the difficulties of individual member states in dealing with complex migration issues in a globalised world and pushed us all towards a renewed effort in this area. in the task force we have worked out a holistic strategy to respond to such problems, recommending more than 30 concrete actions in the areas of cooperation with third countries; regional protection, resettlement and reinforced legal migration; the fight against human smuggling and organised crime; proper management and better surveillance of sea borders; and solidarity with member states experiencing especially high migration pressures. at the same time, we have prepared the ground for debates that may often be less visible but are equally important for the future economic welfare and political relevance of the european union. at the december summit the european council, for the first time ever, discussed concrete defence issues which are so important for our leverage as a political actor and international player. this is a theme i have raised in all my state of the union speeches before you in this parliament. everyone underlined the need for a credible, reinforced and refocused common security and defence policy as a strategic, geopolitical and economic imperative, and there was a consensus on the wish for more cooperation among member states and with our allies, especially nato, and on the obligation to maintain a technological lead in our defence capabilities and our industrial base. from 2001 to 2010, in a rapidly changing and often threatening global context, eu defence spending declined from eur 251 billion to eur 194 billion, meaning that we must do more with less money. we can only do that together. security issues in the broader sense – from energy policy in both its internal and external dimensions, which also remains high on the agenda for the months to come, to cyber security and data protection – are at the heart of the european union’s raison d’être. we share the problems and suffer the threats together, so we are increasingly destined to work out the solutions together. i hope this common european destiny in these and many other areas will be realistically highlighted and strongly defended in the months to come, when the future of the european project will be debated and decided on, and especially during the european elections. we are not yet there, as we will discuss tomorrow a number of important files, and the preparatory work of the commission and the presidency will need to be followed up and brought to a conclusion before the end of this parliamentary term. we still have a lot of work to do, even if – when you think of where we were some time ago and where we are now – we have reason to be confident. let us not forget that, not so long ago, some people were predicting the implosion of the euro and even the disintegration of the european union. and yet now, with consumer and investor confidence resuming, growth – even if it is timid growth – is expected. the recession is behind us, but we should avoid any kind of complacency. with such high levels of unemployment in some of our member states and with many of our companies, especially smes, still lacking the financial means to invest and create jobs, we cannot yet say that we are out of the crisis. but with determination and resolve we can overcome the current challenges. in recent months we have again done a lot of the groundwork in order to do so. 2014, i am sure, will be a year of positive change for the european economy. let us work together for that to happen sooner rather than later.
on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is enough to recall that in just six months 241 legislative acts were adopted, which is two and a half times the average of the previous six months, to highlight the excellent result achieved by this presidency. but the lithuanian presidency has not only stood out in terms of the quantity of concrete results and achievements, but above all in terms of the quality of the work that has been done. lithuania has fully earned the confidence and appreciation of this parliament thanks to the skill and passion of its government and its experts. this was mainly due to the strong europeanism with which the presidency has carried out complex legislative processes, often made even more difficult by eurosceptic and sometimes anti-european political tendencies. the commission has already adopted a proposal for a regulation on the establishment of a european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products for human use. if the funds allocated by the european union for the next seven years can be used from the first days of january, it is also and above all due to the perseverance and commitment of a presidency which has succeeded in making the value of european integration prevail over the selfishness and myopia of some member states. the lithuanian presidency's key role, however, has been in a number of other areas, from the single resolution mechanism for banking crises to the directive on the deposit guarantee scheme. as regards my role as rapporteur, i thank the lithuanian presidency for having broken the political deadlock on the directive on non-financial reporting by companies. i therefore conclude by renewing my congratulations to the lithuanian presidency for reaching very important political agreements which will serve to strengthen the financial, economic and social security of the union, contributing to the development of a strong and inclusive europe.

situation and the banking union, because i believe that we have to look at this issue in the perspective of recent history and of the near future. i remember very well our debates a year ago, both in the next item is the report by robert rochefort, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on a consumer programme 2014-2020 (com(2011)0707 – c7-0397/2011 – 2011/0340(cod)) (a7-0214/2012).
on behalf of the efd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, consumer protection should be a key principle of european action, as laid down in the treaties, whereby the union contributes to the defence of consumers' rights and interests, starting with health, safety and information. the reality of the facts is unfortunately quite different. there is a bloc of countries that does not want these guarantees. the history of the so-called 'made in' mark of origin is plain to see, as are the enormous difficulties in achieving full traceability of the agricultural and food chain. there are those who want to go against the interests of consumers, with obvious harm to both the citizens themselves and to the companies that operate in a regular way, in the light of the sun, that is to say, ensuring compliance with certain criteria of quality, safety and health. without a strong and determined will, this programme, which will take us to 2020, is likely to remain mere propaganda. the financial allocation for its implementation is very low and a large part of it is spent on technical and administrative assistance, not on concrete measures and actions. finally, i would like to see a clearer definition of the role of certain so-called european consumer organizations, which often seem to be more concerned with the interests of large groups and countries than with the interests of the category they are supposed to represent and protect.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i very much agree with one of your opening remarks. the regulation we are talking about seems to be a small thing, but it is in fact a very important solution for the future of the union. we must look at the consumer for what he is: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. and so we can't take them by the hand, lead them as if they were babies, into virtuous behavior. we must give consumers certain rules, and therefore create the conditions in the environment so that they can learn in time what the characteristics of what they decide to consume are. their awareness is the trait we must favour in building the consumer of the future. what has been done in this regulation to this end is very important, including the resources that have been allocated, which will have to grow in the future, to arrive at the new tools, starting with the net, that must be made available to them, to help us in our work and them in their behaviour.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, if more than half of europe's citizens admit that when they buy or consume, they feel neither safe nor protected nor informed, then there is a lot to be done. but unfortunately this programme, while positive, has too little resources. i think that more needs to be done, especially by updating and making a big change in relation to the fact that we need to accompany the level of consumer protection with the growing development of the digital market and e-commerce, which today certainly offers more opportunities - more choice of products and services and possibilities to achieve more savings - but also poses many other problems, legal and technical, and also involves risks and dangers for the uninformed consumer. the consumer's strategic agenda must therefore be more closely linked to the digital agenda and the 'e-buyer' must be trained and equipped. one last note: the commission has also taken the view that the programme should be extended to cover the whole of the community, and that the programme should be extended to cover the whole of the community. vulnerable consumers, children and the most vulnerable citizens need europe to protect them more, to protect their rights even in advance.

in writing. − members of the european parliament may not be sought, detained or prosecuted for opinions or votes expressed in the performance of their duties. that is why i am supporting the immunity request.
mr president, with the crisis, the budget cuts and the constant intensification of world competition, it is appropriate that community funds be used in a targeted, well-targeted and effective way, certainly to the benefit of the local economy but with added value for the whole european economy. it is time to choose the sectors and objectives to be financed in a targeted way, to optimise synergies, instruments and investments, especially in the field of research and innovation - we are talking about horizon 2020 and the structural funds - and then to encourage regions to forge alliances between themselves, especially with research institutes and universities, involving businesses, especially smes, and of course local administrations.
mr president, i supported the winkler report because it provides a sound guide for the commission and the member states to use the structural funds effectively. smart specialisation strategies are the precondition for member states and regions to receive funding from the european regional development fund under the research and innovation goal. it is therefore right to avoid the usual mistakes, to draw on past experience and to make investments pay off: in short, to use these funds in a really structural way. smart specialisation strategies must be based on a broad concept of innovation, not just technological, but also include other measures to stimulate private capital, namely the possibility of finding private international investors. unfortunately, we must acknowledge the serious responsibility of many regions in planning for the next period, because the regions were not consulted before deciding on the areas where innovation was needed, without wasting resources on short-term activities. it is essential that the regions cooperate with each other in accordance with this strategy, thus benefiting from the knowledge of other regions, thus strengthening the european union's competitive position at world level.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because i believe that in a period of economic recession and therefore of budgetary constraints such as the present one, it is absolutely vital that the european union improves its capacity for innovation. the past shows that in the absence of an integrated global strategy, efforts in this area have not achieved the desired results. it is no longer the time for a rainy day in several sectors which are often not connected: the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the information provided by the member states. to ensure that the structural funds are used more efficiently, 11 thematic objectives and several ex ante conditions have been introduced. to receive erdf funding under thematic objective 1, regions will henceforth have to invest in research, development and innovation on the basis of so-called smart specialisation strategies.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report analysing 'smart specialisation: networking excellence for effective cohesion policy'. i believe it is essential to promote innovation strategies at regional and national level which set clear priorities for creating a real competitive advantage. i also share the views expressed in the text, which finally focuses on the potential of small and mediumsized enterprises, which europe too often still underestimates.
in writing. - i express my full support for the report, which deals with a subject with which i am often confronted in my region. it is an indisputable fact that under the pressure of the productive and social crisis, the budgetary difficulties and the sustainability of welfare systems, local governments have often given up on meeting the most difficult challenges of structural reform, to resort to techniques of diverting funds in response to occasional emergencies. the report takes the opportunity of the new framework for the ops to introduce stricter criteria, which give the union greater guarantees on the strategic finalization of the funds allocated; the first is the sharing of good practices (swot matrix, management control) from the private sector, an approach that enhances the vocations of the private production system. finally, i would like to stress the urge to the regions to develop synergy strategies which take advantage of the values of comparative advantage, in particular reindustrialisation policies. i consider particularly serious, at a political level, the inability of local authorities to use the resources available, which leads to the regions spending less than half of the funds allocated. the introduction of stricter specifications will undoubtedly stimulate the development of appropriate strategies and policies.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this resolution on my own initiative, tabled by my group. european funding has not always been used to its fullest potential, due to the absence of an integrated overall strategy to concentrate funds on specific objectives and, above all, to optimise their use. the so-called 'smart specialisation strategies' are therefore necessary, and an ex ante conditionality is a necessary condition for access to erdf funding for r & d. it is essential to identify priorities according to the needs of the various territories, to develop research and innovation strengths and to link them to business needs, avoiding fragmentation of efforts and funding. it is equally important to encourage cooperation with businesses, universities and research centres and higher education institutions.
in writing. - in a time of deep crisis and difficulties it is unthinkable to allow waste or wrong investments. the difficult economic and budgetary situation means that it is no longer possible to distribute 'rainy' funding to many sectors, which are often not linked to each other. in future, greater care will be needed in the choice of objectives to be financed. what do you mean, "what"? by identifying priorities and linking up the relevant actors, paying particular attention to possible synergies between the various promotion instruments at all political levels and developing cooperation with other regions.
in writing. − in the current period of economic crisis and recession, it is crucial for the european union to improve its innovation capacity in a sustainable way, through the adoption of an increasingly integrated global strategy. we support this report, which has identified, with a view to ensuring a more efficient use of the structural funds in future, 11 thematic objectives ('thematic concentration') and several ex ante conditionalities for the allocation of funding. as europe's regions are all different, the smart specialisation strategy will have to be designed to provide opportunities for each of them. efforts will need to focus on cross-sectoral and technology-comprising activities that develop the cross-cutting impact on the entire regional economy. this strategy will have to ensure that synergies and more incentives for investment by the private economy, at local and regional level, or by international investors, arise from the different regional, national and eu concepts and instruments. the strategy should therefore also include measures to stimulate private capital, i.e. the possibility of attracting private international investors, and regional strategies should be documented and include well-thought-out monitoring and evaluation systems.
in writing. - research, development and innovation. these are the key words for the period 2014-2020, when europe absolutely must return to economic growth. the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council at the next meeting of the european council in brussels. the newly adopted text stresses that, in order to receive erdf funds, regions will have to adopt operational programmes focused on smart specialisation strategies. this will be considered a prerequisite for access to european funding and in the absence of a regional and/or national strategy for research and innovation, projects may not be funded, depending on the area of specialisation that may be adopted by region.
in writing. − in a period of economic recession and thus budgetary constraints and steadily increasing global competition, it is vital that the european union sustainably improves its capacity for innovation. in order to ensure that the structural funds are used more efficiently in future, i have therefore decided to vote in favour.
in writing. − innovation and sustainability are the keywords for the european union of the future. however, these two elements only take on practical meaning if they are integrated into an organic, comprehensive and far-sighted strategy, which aims to solve concrete problems rather than defining far-reaching, incremental actions that are far removed from the real problems of european citizens and businesses. for these reasons, i support the elements proposed for the new ris 3 strategy, namely the carrying out of swot analyses identifying specific priorities for research and innovation, the inclusion of measures to stimulate investment, accompanied by reference frameworks and national multiannual plans for priority european projects. all this is accompanied by a system of rational control and surveillance. i agree with the points made by the rapporteur that the strategy should bring about concrete improvements: identify the strengths of each region to invest in, and to connect all relevant actors, from private individuals to local authorities, smes and research centres, in order to manage the promotion programmes and instruments available more efficiently; the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union.
in writing. − past experience has shown that the union's investments, both in general and in research, development and innovation, in the absence of an integrated overall strategy, have often not delivered the expected results. the period of severe economic crisis has also contributed to the obsolescence of the 'rainy day' method of distribution of finance. it is therefore of paramount importance that the union improves its innovation capacity in a sustainable way and exercises greater caution in the choice of objectives to be financed. for these reasons i voted in favour of mr winkler's report, convinced that 'smart specialisation strategies' can make european cohesion policy more effective.

in writing. − i supported mr krahmer's report because i agree with the reduction of the co2 emission limit for new light commercial vehicles from the current 203 g/km to 147 g/km by 2020. this reduction is all the more necessary since light commercial vehicles have a longer life than passenger cars. so producing cleaner vehicles and more reliable methods for co2 emission controls. the regulation is an important tool for combining the implementation of medium-term reduction targets with sufficient predictability for the relevant industry sector.
in writing. − we have approved mr krahmer's proposal to set a co2 emissions target for light commercial vehicles from 2020 onwards. this is the ambitious target of 147 g co2/km, which was already set by the commission in 2011. there is no reason why this strategy should be changed, either from the environmental or the economic point of view. in addition, producers must be given planning assurance so that they can intervene in good time at the design stage to adapt their production to the new standards required. i also think it is important that the 'super credits' have also been retained in the proposal adopted, i.e. those additional credits which any manufacturer can obtain for each vehicle produced which emits less than 50 grams of co2 per kilometre.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the krahmer report on the revision of the co2 regulation for light commercial vehicles. this is a very important regulation, but i hope that it will soon be accompanied by the final adoption of the twin regulation on co2 emissions from passenger cars, which has been the subject of much controversy and a difficult process in the eu council of ministers. the adoption of this regulation strengthens the objective of a significant reduction in co2 emissions from light commercial vehicles by setting an initial target to be reached by 2020 (147g co2 per km) and by prefiguring subsequent targets, the feasibility of which will be decided by the european commission. the regulation also provides for a penalty mechanism for over-running by manufacturers. the regulation adopted today is of course a delicate compromise, and therefore one that can be improved (with more ambitious targets), but one that has the merit of confirming the european union's global leadership in the fight against climate change and contributing to the achievement of significant european-wide targets for the global reduction of co2 emissions.
in writing. - in its measured and realistic approach, the report covers a wide range of issues, including those beyond the regulation under discussion. it is essential to apply a global and result-oriented approach, from wldt alignment to overall environmental budget assessments. to date, fragmentation and contradictions have characterized the approach to these problems, both between member states and at local level; the following measures have been introduced by the regions and metropolitan areas, outside any framework of reference, with paradoxical results: roadworthiness plans that exclude promising vehicles but allow for other higher emission vehicles; urban transport systems converted to electricity, environmentally sustainable, but powered by energy produced in outdated, high-impact power plants. it also seems reasonable to offer general guidelines for development beyond 2020, also with regard to economic and production aspects, thinking not only of vehicle manufacturers (who in any case benefit from exemptions or supercredits), but above all of small commercial and craft enterprises that see this necessary instrumental good increasingly onerous due to fuel costs, or r & d costs or regulations transferred from the producer to the consumer. the report contains indications and measures which are acceptable and i therefore vote in favour of it.

in writing. − as early as 2011, the european parliament and the council adopted a regulation aimed at reducing co2 emissions from new light commercial vehicles. we agree with the rapporteur that this long-term target of 147 g co2/km, to be applied from 2020, should not be changed. this is an ambitious goal that was only agreed in 2011: we therefore intend to confirm the technical feasibility of this, as there has been no change in environmental or economic conditions to justify a change in the level of ambition at this stage. we believe that manufacturers also need planning certainty: further changes at this stage would only undermine this legitimate need for certainty. a change in the target would also undermine the overall credibility of the long-term objectives. although some studies suggest that the 2020 target could be more ambitious, we consider that another factor to be considered is the current economic situation, the financial crisis. we therefore do not think it appropriate to impose on european manufacturers additional economic burdens by setting more ambitious targets.

in writing. - the european parliament, in plenary session today, gave its favourable opinion on the report by mr krahmer on co2 emissions from new light commercial vehicles. the draft law approved will reduce the carbon dioxide emission limit for new light commercial vehicles sold in the union from the current 203 g/km to 147 g/km by 2020. this objective, applicable to companies producing more than 1000 vehicles per year, is an incentive to produce more environmentally friendly models, with a view to a general reduction in co2 emissions in the european transport industries. the technical and structural feasibility of the objective does not impose a significant economic and financial burden on the undertakings to which the regulation is addressed. for this reason, and because of the obvious positive environmental externalities, in a context where 'green' issues are on the agenda, i thought it appropriate to express my favourable opinion of the honourable member's resolution.

in writing. - i believe that an essential element that must be preserved is the mandatory labelling of the origin of processed products. the labelling of origin is of enormous importance for the european market and for consumers. since it has been shown that certain 'low-quality' products are mainly produced in certain regions or countries, this obligation would allow the distribution of quality products on the market and would ensure that the consumer makes an informed choice of the product. on the other hand, labelling must not impose an excessive economic or administrative burden on undertakings: the label must be a symbol of quality, not the result of a bureaucratic process that exceeds the limits of what is feasible. for example, a label should not indicate the origin of each individual ingredient in a product. for these reasons i believe that the commission should continue along the lines set out in its legislative proposal by making the indication of the origin mark compulsory for meat of processed products. at the same time, however, it must balance this obligation with the results of its impact assessment, avoiding excessive costs and administrative burdens for undertakings.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the bartolozzi report because i believe that aromatised wine products are a resource of great importance for the eu, which manages 90% of world production. i think that the rapporteur's decision to accept the commission's proposal for a regulation simplifying regulation 1601/91 and making it clearer is the most appropriate one. in particular, i agree that the european parliament should introduce a number of technical amendments regulating the flavouring, sweetening, colouring and possible addition of alcohol in these products. finally, the privileges granted to national supply chains which distort competition should be reduced and progressively eliminated.
in writing. - i vote in favour. the provisions concerning the definition, designation, presentation, labelling and protection of geographical indications of aromatised wine products needed updating, especially in the light of technological innovation in recent years. however, i would like to stress that it is very important to take account of traditional production methods as well. the new measures applicable to aromatised wine products should also contribute to achieving a high level of consumer protection, to preventing misleading practices and to achieving market transparency and fair conditions of competition.
in writing. the report concerns the replacement of the existing regulation (eec) no 1601/91 by adapting it to the rules of the cmos and the treaty of lisbon. i am voting in favour of the text as the agreements reached concern the definition, designation, presentation and sales denomination of aromatised wines, aromatised wine-based drinks, aromatised wine-product cocktails and the labelling and protection of geographical indications of aromatised wine-product products.
in writing. - as an italian mep, i am particularly interested in everything to do with the wine sector. it is a source of pride and deep pride to see how this sector has managed to weather the shock wave of the economic crisis. these are people who get up every holy morning and work hard to make quality products. it is precisely because of my respect for these workers that we must work to make sure that the european union simplifies their lives by streamlining procedures and clarifying ineffective rules. at the same time, the european institutions have a duty to protect the quality wine sector from external attacks (though unfortunately there is no shortage of internal ones) that undermine the market. the report by mr bartolozzi calls for rapid restructuring of the sector by phasing out ineffective and costly intervention measures and reorientating expenditure to meet consumer demand and make european wine more competitive.
in writing. - today, a further step forward in quality was taken by updating regulation (eec) no 1610/91 on the general rules for aromatised wine products. this is an important issue for the european union, which accounts for about 90% of world production, with traditional production taking root in many member states, especially in the central and southern parts of the continent. this is in the wider context of the simplification of the common agricultural policy, in parallel with the adoption of the single cmo regulation. the aim is to provide consumers with clear information on the nature of products by providing them with a complete picture of geographical indications, definition, designation, presentation and labelling, as well as traditional production methods.
in writing. − flavoured wine products play an important role for consumers, producers and the agricultural sector in general in the european union. they represent a significant share of the european wine sector and constitute a market of great importance from a qualitative and quantitative point of view, both domestically and internationally. we therefore welcome this proposal for a regulation laying down general rules on the definition, designation and presentation of aromatised wines, aromatised wine-based drinks and aromatised wine-product cocktails, since, as well as the protection of geographical indications for these products, it applies to all products placed on the market of the european union, whether produced in the member states or in third countries, as well as to those produced in the union for export. we share the main objectives of: improving the applicability and clarity of eu legislation and introducing a well-defined quality policy for these products; some sales denominations will then be updated in the light of the possibility of increasing the level of wine instead of adding alcohol directly, in order to ensure that the consumer is properly informed and the definitions used are updated to technical developments.
in writing. - i am voting in favour of mr bartolozzi's report, and i intend to support the proposal to improve eu legislation in the wine sector. a specific policy to inform consumers about the technical development of these drinks leads to a better knowledge of the quality they have achieved on the market. the proposal also introduces the need for appropriate labelling of the elements characterising the processing of aromatised wine products, which will improve readability and food information to protect consumers.
in writing. the proposal for a regulation on the definition, presentation, labelling and protection of geographical indications of aromatised wine products aims to simplify and modernise the legislation in this field. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the information on the quality and origin of the product is clearer and more consumer-friendly. in addition, by this regulation, the eu brings the rules on aromatised wine products into line with the requirements of the world trade organisation.
in writing. - i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on the work he has done on this important dossier, which represents an important step forward for consumers, producers and the wine sector in the european union in general. i support the report.
in writing. the regulation adopted today, for which i was rapporteur for the s&d group, aims to update the regulatory framework for an important agricultural product such as aromatised wines. the legislation in force so far dates back to the 1990s and today's vote, while not changing the general purpose of the legislation, introduced amendments to align the specific rules on flavoured wines with the framework regulation (eu) no 1169/2011 on the provision of food information to consumers. clear rules have also been introduced which take account of developments in production methods and the evolution of relevant markets in order to ensure high quality schemes for the products sold and to allow consumers greater clarity and legibility of labelling in order to ensure fully informed purchasing choices.
in writing. - in view of the latest techniques and the increasingly demanding consumer demands, mr bartolozzi's proposal for a regulation simplifies and updates the regulation governing aromatised wine products. the draft regulation concerns primarily measures relating to the designation, presentation and labelling of aromatised wine products, providing for the possibility of indicating the vine variety in the absence of a geographical indication. as regards the technical specifications, the proposal aims, inter alia, to reiterate the exclusivity of the designations established to ensure adequate information for the consumer and to extend the list of sweeteners provided for. the legal aspects of the proposal also call for the provision of rules on geographical indications for aromatised wine products, supplementing those for wine products. i therefore voted in favour of mr bartolozzi's report because i believe that this sector plays a major role for consumers and producers in the agricultural sector in the eu and in italy, representing a significant share of the european and italian wine sector and a qualitatively and quantitatively important market both domestically and internationally.
in writing. the proposal for a regulation on aromatised wines and other wine-based drinks is of great importance for the whole sector in europe, particularly for italy which represents quality products and brands. the legislation affects a whole family of products, of which over 70% of those marketed in the european area are produced in italy. the main objectives are to improve the applicability and clarity of eu legislation on aromatised wine products and to introduce a well-defined quality policy for these products. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that regulation of organic products, information to consumers on labelling, the definition of flavouring, alcoholing, sweetening and colouring processes are important. the existing rules on geographical indications will be aligned with the agreement on trade-related aspects of intellectual property rights (trips agreement) within the wto. i believe that the need to adapt this legislation corresponds to an adaptation to the obligations already assumed by the union, and does not contain rules which have prevented the evolution of the sector and the consolidation of tradition. i hope that the sector, which is affected by this legislation today, will not be penalized by subsequent tax legislation on indirect taxes and excise duties.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report by mr bartolozzi on the geographical indications of aromatised wine products. after some two years of negotiations, a text was reached which improves the applicability, legibility and clarity of the european union legislation on aromatised wine products and introduces a quality policy with very precise rules on protection against any form of false or misleading indication of the origin, composition, content of wine or alcohol, production methods or essential qualities of the products. the new rules on the protection of geographical indications contained in the regulation have taken a step forward in ensuring that the safety of consumers and the production activity in the wine sector are protected at the same time.

in writing. - i am in favour of the report, which provides a clear direction on a matter of urgent revision, without however intending to assume any contrary view. for example, we are aware that the provision of ccs innovation funds, even if obtained from the sale of emission allowances, can be interpreted as a subsidy to fossil fuel consumption and therefore a disincentive to invest in renewables. however, it is undeniable that renewables, also because of their excellent performance, have benefited from important measures and that episodes of retroactive taxation are strongly opposed by the commission and by a large part of this house. nor can we, in discussing ambitious emission reduction targets for 2050, ignore the iea's estimates of the share of fossil fuels in the energy mix up to 2030. ccs technology is proven, economically and environmentally efficient, and simply requires a stable framework with minimal prospects to encourage its industrial deployment. it would be unjustifiable to pass up this opportunity. as the back-loading story has shown, we must reduce the risk of succumbing to complacency, with the result that we find ourselves with a production system that is inadequate to global competition when the negative economic cycle comes to an end.

mr president, ehealth is a great challenge and also an opportunity. as i also stressed in the report on age-related diseases in women, which i was rapporteur for, ehealth can improve access to medical care, which is often not available in hard-to-reach areas, and can improve the quality and frequency of specialist care required by the health conditions of older people, who are often isolated for reasons of mobility. let us not forget that public expenditure on health is increasing, partly because of the ageing of the population. so e-health could save money and improve health care at the same time. accessibility is therefore: but of course also security, legal certainty, control of the online health service, which must be guaranteed and certified; this is obviously for efficiency of service and patient confidence.
in writing. − i voted for this resolution because, although equality should be a fundamental principle in the european union, there is still discrimination concerning the access to the healthcare system. as a matter of fact, the healthcare system is in many cases restricted as a result of financial constraints. i do believe that the ehealth system could play a key role in reducing these inequalities. nonetheless, member states must invest in affordable, high-quality health systems. moreover, some patients are obliged to undergo medical treatment outside their country of residence and this is not acceptable. also, i would like to highlight that every citizen should have the opportunity to use it tools or the skills needed to take advantage of ehealth services and we have the duty to make this possible.
in writing. − the increasing demand for health services due to an ageing population, the mobility of patients and health professionals, the increased expectations of citizens regarding the quality of healthcare and increasingly tight health budgets have led to major challenges for health systems in the european union. e-health, in my view, could be part of the answer to these challenges as a tool to improve access to health services by citizens as well as to reduce waiting times and, above all, to contribute to the achievement of safe, effective and quality healthcare. to achieve those objectives, it is necessary to achieve the interoperability of european health systems and to define at union level certification and authentication schemes for healthcare providers to cooperate with each other, across language and competence boundaries, in order to provide quality services based on patient safety. in order to give citizens and healthcare professionals confidence and belief in the benefits of ehealth applications, it is necessary to provide them with legal certainty: data protection, confidentiality, accountability are key to the establishment of successful ehealth services.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the de lange report, which was adopted by a large majority in the chamber. in recent months a series of food scandals have led to the need to impose harsher sanctions on those who commit food fraud, to the detriment not only of consumers but also of honest producers. in addition to the well-known fraud in relation to horse meat, marketed as beef, i also dealt with rabbit meat as chairman of the committee on petitions. i have received from the italian trade association anlac a report concerning the existence of a parallel import market in italy for rabbits, mainly from china. this trade chain would use certain community countries such as spain and hungary as bases for a trade triangulation. the illegal imported rabbits, often containing antibiotics, would then be sold in italy and the european union as products of italian origin, unbeknownst to italian and european consumers. if this were true, it would be unacceptable harm to consumers and producers: the eu has a duty to investigate and act.
in writing. - as i have already stressed this morning in my speech on the european consumer programme, food fraud is one of the most important issues still to be resolved. all sorts of fraud are certainly deplorable, but in this case we have a not insignificant aggravating factor, due to the fact that here we can have dangerous consequences also from the point of view of human health. the best way to combat this phenomenon would be, on the one hand, to have more frequent and thorough checks and, on the other, to provide for legislative measures that can adequately counter it. the basis for all this must also be the need to achieve a real traceability of the supply chain, from the origin to the consumer, in order to prevent the continuous circumvention of overly permissive rules, which leave room for numerous fraudulent behaviour. italy has long been fighting to protect its production, but it has often found itself alone in europe fighting a battle that goes far beyond the borders of our continent. our country may be the one most affected by this phenomenon, but i believe that this is a matter which must fundamentally concern the whole of europe, because consumers in all other countries are also suffering the damage in the end.
