in writing. - today the european parliament has broken down one of the most symbolic barriers still present in europe in a society which, despite a continuing economic crisis, has sought to look to the future and adapt to the rapid changes in electronic communications. the elimination of roaming charges by 2015 is a significant step towards the creation of a single telecommunications market in europe, an important step towards the effective completion of a genuine internal eu single market. the move towards a single european tariff is therefore a small but significant step in demonstrating that the european union is not just an economic and monetary union and that our participation in europe can bring real added value to citizens through concrete measures that improve and simplify their everyday lives. i also think that the provisions adopted to strengthen the principle of net neutrality, including the prohibition of blocking everyday online services such as skype for economic reasons, are significant. we hope that the council and therefore the governments will be able to confirm definitively the introduction of these important measures for the citizens of europe as soon as possible.
in writing. - first of all, let me say that berec has done well in its institutional tasks, particularly in relation to the measure under consideration today. i also agree with the report, especially where it proposes some important and reinforcing clarifications of the public and social value of the subject in the coordinated text. in this sense, i welcome the forecasts to ensure that services are actually available to citizens, for example in terms of access to technologies that are now integrated into everyday life such as skype, in the face of the tendency shown by some operators to surreptitiously shift demand towards more expensive services. also good is the drastic perimeter of the requirements necessary for the interruption of web communication services: in a liberal form of government, given the right to freedom and confidentiality of communications, it is right that such protocols should be triggered on a case-by-case basis by specific measures of the competent civil or criminal justice body or by documented security and public safety requirements. finally, i see the deadline for free intra-eu roaming as a logical step forward from the previous capping regulation and as one of the cornerstones of the single market, comparable in importance to the first principles of the acquis communautaire, dating back to maastricht.

in writing. - finally, the european parliament has taken a clear position on roaming and net neutrality. the proposal for a regulation is much more complex than that, but i shall simply stress these two aspects. on the first point, i do not understand the european commission's intentions: the so-called roaming iii regulation, which provides, inter alia, for competition only in the roaming sector and allows the addition of another operator to the same sim card only for calls made and received when abroad, came into force less than a year ago. so they asked the telephone companies for investments which less than a year later turn out to be worthless, and that puzzles me. i am rather in favour of abolishing roaming charges to better integrate the internal market. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to cover the whole of the european union, including the european union's external borders. i understand the technical issues that are necessary to allow access to the entire network, but we cannot distort the internet into an elitist project. the commission will continue to work on the development of the network, on the improvement of the cloud, but without stopping the development of more specialised innovations.

in writing. - today's vote expresses the will to create a single telecommunications market. the european project is to abolish roaming charges by 1 july 2016. telephone companies will not be allowed to charge higher rates for calls made within europe and will be prohibited from charging a special rate for calls received in roaming. this is the europe we like, which protects consumers, takes account of the needs of citizens and guarantees new rights for consumers, harmonised throughout the community, offering more transparency in contracts and advantages for traders thanks to a simplification of the legislation which they will be able to take advantage of to operate in the 28 member states.

in writing. - more than 200 telephone operators follow different rules and offer different rates to their customers, a fragmented market of 510 million european citizens. i voted in favour of the new package of new rules which will have a significant impact on the telecommunications market. i support the abolition of roaming charges from 15 december 2015 and the fact that internet providers will no longer be able to block or slow down the services of their competitors. protecting the right to neutral access to the internet means protecting the internet itself with its characteristics of openness and innovation. in this case, legal certainty is guaranteed by defining the rights of final consumers and the obligations of telecommunications operators which result from them. it therefore remains essential that the provision of specialised services is based on strict guarantees in order to safeguard the quality and neutrality of network access. i also believe that early withdrawal charges are unfair and arbitrary and are imposed by traders to force consumers into a contract.
in writing. - the abolition of roaming for voice, sms and data services is a major milestone in the completion of the internal market and has a strong symbolic value, as it will remove a significant financial burden on european citizens. in this sense, the principle of openness and freedom of access to the internet, a fundamental pillar for the proper development and completion of the european market, becomes fundamental. i also support and agree with the emphasis on the freedom to provide electronic communications throughout the union, but as this is a very complex subject, great care must be taken in the implementation of this system. as regards the proposals on wholesale access products and quality assured service, a general consultation is likely to be needed to better understand how to proceed on the subject.
in writing. - the european parliament has repeatedly stressed the importance of the security of electronic services. there is currently no comprehensive union cross-border and cross-sector framework ensuring secure, reliable and user-friendly electronic transactions, including electronic identification, authentication and trust services. the existing union legislation, namely directive 1999/93/ec on a community framework for electronic signatures, is limited to electronic signatures only. the adoption of rules to ensure the mutual recognition of electronic identification and authentication across the union is one of the key actions of the roadmap for stability and economic growth. in this context, while welcoming the commission's proposal and welcoming the efforts to establish a legal framework at union level in this area, i nevertheless believe that the objectives and content of the proposed regulation should be further clarified. in my view, the commission's proposal, in its present form, is too vaguely defined to be adequately assessed by the legislator. with regard to electronic identification schemes, i agree with the rapporteur that it is desirable to achieve technical interoperability between member states without significantly altering the national solutions chosen by individual countries, depending on their specific characteristics.
in writing. - i found the report balanced and concrete, not to mention that the potential benefits of this measure are enormous. online trade could become more reliable and an undertaking could participate electronically in a public procurement procedure initiated by a member state or sign contracts electronically with entities located in other member states. i therefore voted in favour of the text.
in writing. - when it comes to promoting innovation, we cannot forget the business generated daily on the internet. of course, e-commerce is not the only area to invest in, but allowing physical barriers to be removed undoubtedly rewards the most competitive firms. there are two areas that are still unresolved and apparently need regulatory intervention because the market either cannot or will not find the solutions on its own, and those are delivery services and online payment services. we have already dealt with the former recently, while this proposal for a regulation aims to update the existing directive and bring it up to date. the proposal achieves both objectives effectively and in a timely manner, by strengthening the internal market with the legal instrument chosen and safeguarding the interests of consumers on the one hand and of businesses on the other. for these reasons i have helped to get this proposal approved.

in writing. - the 2008 financial crisis raised doubts about the proper functioning of the european audit regime, especially with regard to public-interest entities. the weaknesses in the banking sector are clearly attributable to insufficient supervision and inadequate regulatory safeguards. whether and to what extent better audit rules could have averted the crisis is debatable, but a more robust audit process and a more dynamic audit market are undoubtedly a better guarantee of control. for the purposes of this report, due consideration has been given to issues relating to improving the quality of audit services and competition in the audit market and to the approximation of the rules of practice in the eu. the attention paid to the costs for firms and investors, the users of audit services, who must strike a balance between costs and benefits, is also appreciated. in some cases, however, the proposals represent an unreasonable burden on firms and introduce side-costs with uncertain benefits. the quality of auditing needs to be at the top of any reform, as stakeholders and investors need to have confidence in the system to continue investing in companies.
in writing. - i share and support the objectives underlying the commission's proposal and support the choice to pursue a maximum level of harmonisation for public interest entities (pis) through the adoption of the regulatory instrument. highly harmonised rules on independence and the prevention of conflicts of interest for the audits of pis are fundamental elements for a proper statutory audit. i also support the obligation to rotate audit firms regularly and greater cooperation between the competent authorities and between the competent authorities and the european securities and markets authority (esma), which should be the backbone of supervision at european level and for which i would have preferred a stronger role.
in writing. - as there are very serious doubts as to whether the proposal in question can adequately guarantee the independence and autonomy necessary for the proper performance of the audit task, i abstained.

in writing. - it is desirable that voluntary audits should be excluded from the application of the audit provisions as currently provided for, because the commission proposal would involve a higher cost and an additional administrative burden for small and mediumsized enterprises. at a very particular moment, when our companies are doing everything possible to get out of the crisis, it is not conceivable to give them an additional economic burden to bear. furthermore, while additional access to capital may help smaller audit firms to close the gap with major international networks, the removal of the majority of voting rights requirements for statutory auditors, which allows a third party to hold such a majority, risks undermining the independence of the profession.

the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the agri-food industry in the european union is the second most important sector, with a total output of the food chain of some 750 billion euros a year, employing over 48 million people, from primary production to retail trade and catering. official controls in the food chain are essential to ensure a high level of health protection and the proper implementation of the legislation governing the agri-food chain. they also help to maintain the high reputation of european products in the international context. the european union's ability to export to third countries is also based on high safety standards which add value. the legislative proposal for which i am the rapporteur is part of the legislative package published on 6 may and is based on the principle of checks commensurate with the risk and aims to create a single and harmonised framework of procedures and checks. i thank all my colleagues, and especially mr schnellhardt, for their intensive and constructive cooperation. the work done in recent months has enabled us, through over a thousand amendments, to make the text clearer so as not to leave room for different national interpretations which have often been the cause of uneven application by the competent authorities. the text to be voted on tomorrow introduces the principle of minimum frequency of inspections in all sectors of the food chain to avoid disparities between member states. in the milk sector, some countries carry out checks every ten years, while others carry them out annually. only by harmonizing the frequency of checks can we restore consumer confidence, especially after the various scandals, not least the one concerning horse meat. this has included the creation of reference centres for the authenticity and integrity of the food chain. official controls should be independent and unannounced in order to safeguard their effectiveness at the time of verification. thanks to the cooperation of all the political groups, article 15 on meat production explicitly incorporates haccp and hygiene procedures. the auxiliary staff may assist the veterinarian during official inspections, but the responsibility remains with the veterinarian. many countries have reduced the budget for controls and it has therefore become necessary to keep the payment of fees compulsory, but with some flexibility for member states. the collection of the fees will help, together with the financial resources of the states, to carry out the checks which - i stress - are fundamental for food safety. the commission's proposal provided for exemption of smes from the payment of the compulsory tariffs, but the criteria identified appeared too broad and would have exempted about 90% of the companies, making it unsustainable for the competent authorities to carry out the checks. the exemption for micro-enterprises, with more restrictive parameters, should be maintained and some of the amendments tabled in plenary are in this direction. finally, i welcome the report which the committee on the environment has rejected and i hope that it will be voted on by a large majority tomorrow.
the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a fire. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am firmly convinced that the structure of the new regulatory framework proposed by the commission will ensure greater efficiency and consistency in the conduct of controls in all sectors of the agri-food chain in the european union. although controls on plant reproductive material and plant health controls are by nature different from those provided for in the livestock sector, the fundamental objective is to achieve better harmonisation and simplification across all sectors and to create a common regulatory framework in the organisation of official controls along the entire agri-food chain. i think that the text adopted by our committee on energy, research and technology is a good compromise. we must not forget that seeds and plants are the crucial, if not the vital, starting point of this supply chain and are therefore an integral part of the new regulation on official controls. the european seed guidelines include specific rules on official controls. in this respect, it is essential that there should be an appropriate level of control for all categories of seeds so that farmers can find high quality seeds on the market and use them, thereby supporting the agricultural production system from the ground up. i believe, however, that these controls should also be lightened for small farms.
i would like to thank the rapporteur and the shadow rapporteurs from both the committee on agriculture and the committee on the environment, as well as my former colleague, francesca barracciu, who has been following this dossier for the socialist and democratic group before me. the document on animal health which is being discussed in the house today has broad and cross-cutting support on the most significant points. we have managed to meet the information needs of citizens and consumers, farmers and trade associations by eliminating burdensome obligations and requirements and by allowing derogations based on the specific characteristics of individual countries, while at the same time excluding them from those areas - such as the transport of animals - which are most at risk for the spread of diseases and by enhancing the training and prevention role that trade associations can play. for the member states we have differentiated the rules between compulsory and voluntary programmes for the eradication of diseases, in the clear sense of subsidiarity. we have also been able to strengthen the references to animal welfare and antimicrobial resistance, which are creating increasing difficulties in the fight against animal diseases, and to ensure the european parliament's co-decision role in relation to a proposal from the commission which is too self-referential. the balance that has been struck must be defended and the elements which have been proposed in several amendments but which do not fall within the scope of this regulation are not acceptable, even though we recognize the freedom of members and groups to take a different line. in particular, as regards cloning, in line with the decision of the committee on agriculture, while leaving a vote, we are against it because it is not relevant to the subject of this regulation. i also think that the eight-hour limit in the transport sector should not be included here. this new regulation brings together a number of sources of legislation and we hope to give effect to the principles by delegating to other acts. we are convinced that a great step forward is being made and we expect the council to adopt its position which we will convey to the future parliament.
on behalf of the efd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, when it comes to health, there is never too much attention. although it is an animal health proposal, its scope has a tangible impact on public health as a whole: in fact, about 70 percent of infectious diseases are common to animals and humans. prevention can be seen as the keyword for effective management of animal diseases. it can be achieved, for example, through the adoption and dissemination of good animal husbandry practices and through the responsible use of veterinary medicinal products. prevention, however, is not always sufficient to prevent the emergence of certain diseases, especially in the wildlife sector. their movements and interactions follow the laws of nature and therefore cannot be controlled. it is in this context that monitoring measures play a vital role and it is here that i would like to emphasize the positive role played by hunters and their hunting associations. the hunter is one of the most immediate warning signals we have on the territory and, above all, at no cost to the community. hunters are often the first to come across infected wildlife and are immediately reported to the competent authorities who in turn activate the required enforcement measures. their knowledge is proven by a series of meticulous courses and examinations, which also have to be passed in the field of animal health. knowledge is then supplemented by experience handed down from generation to generation. finally, it is misleading to say that live hunting calls should be banned because they are a vehicle for diseases that cannot be monitored. on the contrary, the use of poultry traps could indeed be a valuable tool for monitoring the health of wild birds, as happened during the avian influenza epidemic. we are going beyond the banal prohibitionist slogans and making intelligent collaboration our goal.
member of the commission. - madam president, honourable members, i have listened carefully to the debate with great interest. of course, there is the usual debate about whether we should control more or control less. i think that the commission’s proposal and also many of the amendments submitted are a reasonable compromise. first of all, may i say that we did draw lessons from the horsemeat scandal. i think it is unfair to state that the commission did not do anything. in fact, we introduced a number of measures, including a food fraud network within the member states, an it system to report fraud, we have increased the penalties, we have more sampling plans and we have also set up a food fraud section within sanco. the horsemeat scandal is of course just one incident which happened because of fraudulent labelling and which affected an entire market of 500 million. and this is the problem: that it is a single market and therefore anything which evades the rules of importation as regards food safety affects the entire market, which is why i agree with those members of parliament who have said that we must be more vigilant on imports. at the same time, we maintain the so-called open system, because we have signed the international plant protection convention and also have obligations under the wto which oblige the contracting parties to base their phytosanitary legislation on identified pest risks to plant health. incidentally, concerning the comment made regarding the russian ban on pigmeat, and animal health, the members of parliament will be pleased to know that last monday the commission initiated the first step against russia in the wto. i think anyone who has joined the wto has to accept their obligations, including the obligations of regionalisation. if two wild boar infected with african swine fever cross over from belarus into poland, only that infected area should be affected, not the entire polish territory or, even worse, the entire eu territory. so i think that, because of this, it was right and proper to initiate proceedings against russia through the wto arbitration procedure. the question which has been raised by some meps is: should fees linked to official controls be mandatory or should we leave this question entirely in the hands of the member states? there are two reasons why we at the commission think that this choice should not be offered. first of all, to achieve harmonisation and thus create a level playing field across member states, i think that the competent authorities should be required to take the same costs into account. that is to say, the fees should be based on the costs, both direct and indirect, rather than being a tax. the fees should only be intended to recover the cost of the control and nothing more. i also think that, if member states are entitled to consider the costs they want, this would allow the perpetration of divergent and potentially distortive practices. operators in the richer member states could be advantaged, as these member states would either not impose fees or impose lower fees while operators in less rich member states would pay relatively more. apart from which, as i said, micro-enterprises – which amount to 80% of operators – will be excluded from these fees. i agree with those who say that animal welfare is important but it should not be included in this legislation. i think that the commission has already shown its commitment in this regard. not only have we taken the first preparatory steps for a general animal welfare law, but it was this commission which prohibited the marketing of animal-tested cosmetics in the european union. we have also enforced the legislation regarding pregnant sows and laying hens’ cages, and only recently we launched for the first time our cloning proposal. should there be more amr in this proposal? i think there should be more amr, but not in this proposal. we have already launched an action plan in this regard and one should also say that the proposal that we have before us is only one element of the eu’s fight against antibiotic resistance. we have a proposal now which is forthcoming on veterinary medicines which will be a crucial part of it, that is to say, that we should not abuse antibiotics even in animal health, thus endangering, as some meps have said, human health also. 25 000 people in the eu die every year because of infections which are resistant to antibiotics. at the same time, i would advise against certain amendments to this proposal which, as some have said, are outside its scope and stray into the regulation of veterinary medicines. i hope that rapid progress can be made in the next parliament towards a second-reading agreement at the earliest possible opportunity.

the rapporteur. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, transparency by the european institutions in their dialogue with civil society is a fundamental principle enshrined in the treaties. for european democracy to function properly, and to avoid the power of the few over the interests of the many, the activities of interest groups wishing to make their voices heard in the legislative process must be transparent and follow strict and rigorous rules of conduct. the amendments to the interinstitutional agreement, which parliament negotiated with the commission, are a step in this direction. but it is only a partial step forward, especially in relation to parliament's request for the establishment of a compulsory register. we are aware that there is no legal basis in the treaties, but there is a flexibility clause which makes it possible to make the union's powers consistent with its objectives, and parliament is strongly calling for it to be used in the next legislature if there is no revision of the treaties. parliament also asked the council to join the register. even within the limits of a voluntary mechanism based on incentives, the new agreement does contain some progress compared to the past and the resolution preceding the text of the agreement underlines and clarifies these. the registrant will have to declare all clients for whom he/she lobbies, clearly linking each activity with each client. the rules of the code of conduct are made more stringent to limit non-compliance or abuse as much as possible. we have endeavoured to clarify the role of former members, requiring that they do not use the benefits of their status if they are engaged in activities covered by the scope of the register. the incentives for registration - this is important - are also and above all conceived in the resolution as disincentives for those who do not register in relation to the currently very wide freedom of action allowed to lobbyists. the european commission is being asked to be as ambitious and as strict as parliament has decided to be. the question of the role of law firms is further clarified by distinguishing between legal aid activities and those covered by the register. it is good that some associations of law firms of lawyers want to accept this principle, and we must continue to work on it. another important issue that has emerged is that of the municipalities. i would point out that mayors and representatives of those institutions will not have to register, but permanent representative offices will have to do so. it may be useful to clarify and clarify this in the guidelines that follow. as regards the amendments - some of which will be accepted - there is the question of the legislative footprint. i would like to express my opinion on this: i think that a mandatory mechanism would risk having a counterproductive effect and thus encouraging lobbying to get one's name registered in the approved reports. we can consider the proposal for another amendment, a voluntary mechanism, on which i am ready to hear the suggestions that will emerge in the debate. on the whole, however, i believe that, within the limits of the existing treaties and a difficult negotiation, parliament has made a step forward and that the new register will strengthen transparency and thus the rights of all citizens.
member of the commission. - madam president, first of all let me again clarify the question of the regions in europe. the regions in europe will not be expected to register in the future, and the status quo will therefore be upheld in regard to them. it is true that this registration is not yet mandatory, but i believe that we have strengthened significantly the incentives to join the transparency register, and the commission will assess the results of this approach in due course. on law firms, i can say that there are consultations with the council of bars and law societies of europe, which reveal that they are open to enter into discussions with the institutions in order to find a workable compromise so that lawyers can sign up to the register. on the question of the assistance we give to ngos, which will be recorded in this transparency register, yes, we do have strict financial controls on what eu funds they use and how they use them, and whether they use them according to the intention for which they were given. i do not think that there is jurisdiction to see what they get from other sources, unless of course it affects their independence of judgment and the impartiality of the judgment itself. i look forward to more cooperation in this regard on something which is of interest to european citizens, and i think that this proposal will clearly result in improving the register further.
the rapporteur. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i think that the debate has shown a broad unity in parliament on a number of important points. firstly, there is the problem of an anomalous, asymmetrical situation, compared with the current weight and strength of lobbying in the european parliament, which is liable to jeopardize the balanced development of democracy in europe. the question of transparency is therefore fundamental. secondly, we deplore the absence of a compulsory register, and we are all united on this point. we are aware, of course, that the present legal basis does not allow this, but we point out a concrete way of building this legal basis and we call on the commission to pursue it with determination and speed. finally, as long as we remain within the framework of an optional register, i would like to stress to my colleagues the importance of the question of incentives as disincentives - this is a fundamental element. it is therefore important to give clear instructions to the bureau of parliament on how to reduce the margin of manoeuvre for those who do not register, and this is not to further encourage and facilitate the lobbying of those who do register. this is a discriminatory point which the report clarifies and interprets in the right way. as far as law firms are concerned, i think that article 10 of the amended agreement makes very clear the difference not in the status of lawyers but in the activity they carry out. so i think that all the activities of law firms which fall within the scope of lobbying must lead to registration and those who do not register must not enjoy the incentives and thus fall within the system of disincentives which we want to build in parliament. i think we can work together on these points and i think we can also be open to a number of amendments which aim to improve our report even further.

vice-president of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank parliament once again, and in particular the rapporteurs and the shadow rapporteurs of the imco committee, for the work they have done on the package on product safety and market surveillance. i have appreciated the energy and attention which parliament has devoted to this very important dossier for the proper functioning of the internal market in products. the package, which bears my signature and that of commissioner mimica, is a fundamental step towards improving the application of product legislation in the internal market, mainly for two reasons. first, because it ensures the effective protection of all the public interests that our rules are intended to safeguard: the health and safety of consumers and professional users and the environment. secondly, because compliance with eu legislation guarantees the conditions of fair competition which are indispensable to prevent honest and lawful undertakings from being subjected to unfair competition by non-standard products. i shall concentrate my remarks on the regulation on market surveillance, while commissioner mimica will deal with those on the safety of consumer products. i would like to inform the rapporteur, mrs pietikäinen, that the commission welcomes many of the amendments proposed by the european parliament, because they are in the right direction and in line with the spirit of the proposal. i am referring, for example, to the introduction of a clearer distinction between non-compliant products and products presenting a risk. we also support the introduction of guiding principles to increase the effectiveness of market surveillance controls and the general objective of strengthening surveillance in the field. finally, we look with interest at the proposed obligations for internet service providers, while noting that their exact wording must remain fully consistent with european e-commerce legislation. we have some reservations, however, about certain other amendments, in particular the proposal that the commission should assess the resources and programmes of the national market surveillance authorities. the latter would cause an excessive bureaucratic burden and an intrusion into the administrative organization of the member states. parliament also called for the commission to establish a pan-european database on all types of accidents. it is true that accurate accident and incident statistics would help to set priorities for market surveillance, but the collection of relevant data is by no means an easy task and a cost-benefit analysis would be required before deciding on this proposal. finally, parliament proposed a number of principles for determining the administrative sanctions to be imposed on those responsible for infringements. the commission broadly shares and supports the spirit of these amendments. in this connection, as announced in our communication of 22 january, we are considering the advisability of a legislative proposal to harmonise economic sanctions throughout the internal market for industrial products. i must point out, however, that the obligation to publish a blacklist of economic operators who have repeatedly infringed the provisions of the regulation would be difficult to implement. before concluding, i would like to make one last comment on the other part of the package, the part concerning product safety, in particular the obligation to indicate the origin of the product. as you know, i attach great importance to this element of the package and i thank the rapporteur, mrs schaldemose, for her statements in this debate and for supporting the commission's position. i agree that the indication of the origin of products would make it easier for the authorities and consumers to find information on the supply chain. this is important for traceability and, consequently, for ensuring product safety and conformity. it also serves to improve confidence in the single market, because transparency of market conditions and greater consumer choice can only benefit operators who act responsibly. for these reasons, i appreciated the support received from the imco committee and the work done by the rapporteur, mrs schaldemose, and the shadow rapporteurs. i also recall that parliament has spoken on several occasions and i thank it in favour of the indication of origin: through the resolutions of december 2010 and february 2011, the schaldemose report and the inta and imco committees, which had already called for the adoption of traceability labelling to determine the country of origin of products. in addition, as recently as last january, parliament expressed its regret at the withdrawal of the so-called 'made in' proposal. the indication of origin was included in the current package in response also to parliament's calls: the commission has thus gone from words to deeds. we hope that parliament will continue to support us, and we are counting on it today in favour of article 7 of the rules of procedure, as requested by mrs schaldemose.
member of the commission. - mr president, let me begin by thanking parliament and, in particular, the rapporteurs, ms schaldemose and ms pietikäinen, for their fast and fruitful work and overall support for the product safety and market surveillance package. it is clear that we share a common goal: enhanced consumer safety and better functioning of the internal market, based on four clear principles and priorities: a simpler legal framework fit for its purpose; flawless identification and traceability of products; clear responsibilities of economic operators; and effective enforcement by authorities. both the commission’s proposals and the amendments by the committee on the internal market and consumer protection aim to reinforce the key elements of this important legislation. i will focus my intervention on the regulation on consumer product safety, as vice-president tajani has already commented on the market surveillance proposal. let me underline that the commission can support most of the internal market committee’s amendments. for example, we could support the introduction of an explicit reference to the precautionary principle, which has for a long time been a guiding principle for eu decision-making. we also understand parliament’s concerns about products that appeal to children, and we support the opportunity to address this in the context of the safety assessment of non-harmonised products. we also welcome your general support for the mandatory origin-making proposal. in this regard, i am confident that the council will soon be in a position to enter into trialogues on the entire package. however, the commission does have concerns about certain other amendments. firstly, the proposed ‘eu safety tested’ label. the commission is not convinced that an additional safety marking on products – even a voluntary one – would add value for european consumers or reinforce their safety. rather, it may increase confusion, contradict certain parts of eu legislation on ce marking and, potentially, bring the application of testing with no extra benefits. secondly, our concerns are related to trademark protection. indeed, europe needs to take effective measures against intellectual property rights violations. however, this should remain a subject of specific eu legislation and should not be mixed up with product safety regulation. thirdly, our joint objective is to simplify the current rules. this means laying down a common set of obligations for economic operators across sectors, strictly in line with the existing framework for the marketing of products. any amendments that introduce additional obligations for non-harmonised consumer goods could jeopardise this objective. finally, the commission acknowledges that stricter rules on penalties could contribute to the effectiveness of market surveillance. however, the proposed ceiling for administrative penalties and a possible blacklist could be counterproductive. with these points in mind, i want to conclude by confirming the commission’s readiness to work closely with parliament and the council to reach agreement on the two regulations as soon as possible. on a separate note, i would like to thank mr weidenholzer and his shadow rapporteurs for their intensive work on the report on consumer utilities. i welcome the final agreement reached. it recognises that consumer protection is already well embodied in eu legislation for the sectors identified, but it also gives us useful guidelines for addressing the remaining challenges. in this regard, let me remind you of some ongoing activities of the commission. firstly, the connected continent proposal that you strongly supported aiming to strengthen end users’ rights concerning many of the key issues identified in your report. secondly, our work with stakeholders on the reliability of comparison tools, price transparency and clear billing, especially in the energy sector. thirdly, our ongoing study on consumer vulnerability patterns in key sectors and our constant efforts to make sure the existing consumer protection legislation is effectively implemented. finally, the commission is continuing its intense work with consumers’ organisations, both at eu and national level. i am confident that all these actions will also contribute to better protection of consumers in the utility markets.

in writing. - the establishment of a single bank resolution authority for the countries participating in the single supervisory mechanism and at the same time a single resolution fund is an important step towards transferring the management of banking crises from the national to the european level. i believe that this changeover, which follows the centralisation of supervisory powers at the ecb, is fundamental to safeguarding our common market and our single currency. the crisis, with its devastating and protracted effects, has demonstrated certain weaknesses in our financial system and has seriously called into question its sustainability and, in some ways, the sustainability of the european union as a whole. it is a long and complex process it will take eight years to complete but it can really be a pillar for the europe of the future.
in writing. - i voted in favour of mrs ferreira's report, in line with the ppe. the proposed regulation aims to create a banking union in the eu to increase financial stability and ensure that the eu economy can rely on a functioning financial sector. the regulation establishes a single resolution mechanism (srm) which will apply to the euro area member states and other member states that have chosen to participate in it in order to complete the banking union. the purpose of the srm is to apply identical rules to all banks and to provide effective procedures to deal with bank failures while minimising the cost to taxpayers and the economy. the srm will complement the single supervisory mechanism (ssm), under which the ecb takes ultimate responsibility for the supervision of all banks in the euro area. the commission also proposed a european parliament and council directive to create a framework for the reorganisation and resolution of credit institutions and investment firms. this will mean that member states, whether or not they choose to participate in the srm, will have to apply the same rules on prudential and resolution requirements for banks.
in writing. - i did not support the ferreira report which analyses the proposal for the creation of a single crisis resolution mechanism for the banking union. the legislation under discussion is part of the european banking union, which i have many reservations about, because i do not believe it will help europe to emerge from the economic crisis in which it has been for too many years.
in writing. - i supported the proposal because it aims to create a single bank resolution authority for the countries that join the single supervisory mechanism. the purpose of the single mechanism is to apply the same set of rules to all credit institutions in the participating member states, thus providing effective procedures to deal with banking crises and minimising the costs to taxpayers and the economy. a single resolution fund for banks in crisis is also being set up together with the board, which will be financed by contributions of 1% of the value of its deposits. it is expected that, at the end of a transitional period of 10 years, the fund will be able to count on approximately eur 55 million. the regulation aims to shift crisis management powers to the european level. the resolution fund will reach its planned level of resources over a transitional period of eight years, during which time the resources paid by banks in the same member state will gradually become mutualisable (i.e. usable for any banking crisis), until complete mutualisation is achieved.
in writing. - i think this is a late and insufficient measure, considering what has happened in recent years and the crisis situation in which we are still found. in a single currency logic, which proved to be a controversial and problematic choice, more should have been done to avoid the fragmentation of the union's financial market. does it still make sense to intervene with these kinds of measures today? should we not reconsider the choice of a single currency? we are also talking about a fund that will have 55 billion in 2024, at full capacity: during the 2008-12 crisis, banks were bailed out by governments with almost 600 billion in payments and 4,300 billion in guarantees.
in writing. - after months of heavy handedness and a final 16-hour negotiation that ended at dawn, we can say that parliament has made some important points. we have reduced the time taken to complete the single european resolution fund to eight years. we will have started from 1 january 2015 the merging of 40% of national resources into the single fund; this will have to rise to 60% in the following year and to 70% by january 2017. so by 2017, the single resolution fund will be 'close to full operation', reaching the figure of 55 billion. the bail-in will not apply to deposits up to €100,000. but parliament also got protection for at least three months for an account temporarily holding more than €100,000, such as in the case of a house sale. the role of parliament was also decisive in improving a mechanism which could have been and which we would have liked to have been more courageous, but which nevertheless represents a fundamental guarantee for european taxpayers who will no longer have to bear the costs of any banking crises.
in writing. - this is an essential element of the banking union. the proposal aims to preserve the integrity of the member states participating in the single supervisory mechanism (ssm) by introducing a single resolution mechanism (srm) to deal with failing banks. the srm will allow uniform rules to be applied to any bank in difficulty in a participating member state and will allow for effective progress towards the resolution of bank failures in a way that minimises the cost to the taxpayer and the real economy. the structure of the srm ensures that the decision-making process is streamlined and fast. the tasks of the srm shall be shared between the commission and the national resolution authorities.
in writing. - the proposal for a regulation was submitted by the european commission in july 2013. it aims to create a single bank resolution authority for the countries that join the single supervisory mechanism. a single resolution fund is also set up alongside the board, funded by the banks themselves, to cover the costs of resolution. the regulation thus aims to shift the powers of supervision to the ecb and the powers of crisis management to the european level, in order to avoid that the exercise of supervision powers at supranational level is not matched by resolution powers and crisis costs at the same level. the resolution fund will reach its planned level of resources over a transitional period of eight years (starting on 1 january 2016), during which the resources paid by banks in the same member state will gradually become mutualizable (i.e. usable for any banking crisis, regardless of the country of incorporation of the failing bank) until full mutualization.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the report on the technical requirements for inland waterway vessels, in line with the ppe. directive 2006/87/ec lays down the criteria and technical requirements for the issuing of navigation certificates valid for all inland waterways in the union. the commission is thus seeking to ensure the highest possible level of safety for inland navigation. the commission's objective is to further harmonise the technical requirements for inland waterway vessels and to intensify cooperation between the actors involved in order to increase efficiency and legal clarity in a sector mainly composed of smes. the inland waterway fleet is extremely sustainable due to its long life cycle. i agree with the rapporteur that further environmental benefits in terms of air pollutants could be achieved if the propulsion of the fleet were gradually renewed and adapted to new technologies. at the same time, i believe that a structured policy with realistic short and medium-term objectives would be the winning strategy for a sector with great potential. the certainty of the legal framework is undoubtedly the first step in encouraging investment and thus ensuring the sustainable development of the inland waterway market.
in writing. - while i share some of the views expressed in the wortmann-kool report on the technical requirements for inland waterway vessels, i must point out that the text is more focused on the needs of the countries of central europe than on our own territories and overly emphasizes the need to renew river vessels for greater environmental efficiency, which would bring additional costs to companies already in serious difficulty because of the protracted crisis. for these reasons i have decided to abstain.
in writing. - the commission proposes to further harmonise the technical requirements for inland waterway vessels. i believe that the efforts made to use the technical expertise of the ccnr should be supported, but it remains to be examined whether the current proposal is fully in line with the new framework for cooperation between the commission services and the ccnr on technical standards. the technical annexes have not been amended, as the aim of the proposal is to create a framework which will allow the development of a unified body of standards which can be used by the eu, the ccnr and, subsequently, other international organisations. amending the technical requirements would create further confusion and legal uncertainty and would be counterproductive to the purpose of the proposal. in addition, the development or revision of technical requirements for inland waterway vessels requires technical expertise and extensive coordination between the ccnr, eu member states and third countries.
in writing. - the european shipping industry, in particular inland waterway transport, is made up of a large number of small and mediumsized enterprises, both in manufacturing and in transport. it was therefore necessary to find a common ground in european legislation on this subject and to harmonise the rules in this area. the text on technical requirements for inland waterway vessels provides legal clarity on the principles governing this sector, and i therefore voted in favour.
in writing. - further harmonisation of technical requirements for inland waterway vessels and increased cooperation between the river commissions, the united nations economic commission for europe and the commission are two key objectives which will improve the efficiency and clarity of inland waterway legislation. i also appreciate that the report emphasizes the additional environmental benefits, particularly with regard to the gradual renewal of the fleet's propulsion.
in writing. - fraud linked to false declarations of origin of goods results in annual losses of eur 100 million per year in the eu-27. the proposal aims to protect consumers and the internal market, and to simplify and speed up the mechanisms for combating customs fraud. unnecessary and repetitive bureaucracy must be abolished in favour of strengthening and securing the internal market and the products circulating within it, thus ensuring a high level of consumer protection. achieving tangible results requires legal certainty and effective prevention and detection mechanisms at national and eu level, as well as close cooperation between these levels.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because i believe that it is appropriate to encourage mutual assistance between the administrative authorities of the member states and cooperation with the commission to ensure the correct application of customs and agricultural legislation. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods are respected. in the light of the impact assessment carried out by the commission, it appears that customs officials have no means of verifying the veracity of the information declared on the goods to be transported. there is de facto abuse of the transit procedure which is monitored by documentary checks and visual inspections, which are however limited in scope. fraud linked to false declarations of origin or false descriptions of transported goods results in considerable annual losses for the eu. moreover, the increased level of fraud undermines consumer safety: effective prevention and detection mechanisms at national and eu level are therefore indispensable. the imco committee's proposal aims to speed up the mechanisms for combating customs fraud and avoiding excessive bureaucracy, to increase the security of the internal market and of the products circulating within it, and to ensure, at the same time, a high level of consumer protection.

in writing. - i am of course in favour of all measures which can serve to eliminate, or at least to limit, fraud linked to a false declaration of origin at customs. customs officials often have no means of verifying that the declared origin of the goods actually corresponds to the itinerary of the container in question and cooperation between the various authorities in this field is still too weak. this is a huge problem, with significant economic damage: in 2011 alone, member states reported losses of around eur 107.7 million due to misrepresentation of goods carried, and these are cases of fraud detected, suggesting a much wider range of illegality. the proposal under consideration should make checks simpler, but at the same time more effective, also making use of the new technologies at our disposal. those who commit these types of crimes harm not only consumers, misleading them about the true origin of a product, but also honest producers and distributors who operate by the rules and who find themselves competing in a distorted market.

madam president, with this directive on alternative fuels infrastructure we are taking an important step forward because we have reached a balanced compromise that marries a non-ideological environmental culture capable of combining sustainability with development, growth, the market and business. these are ambitious but realistic and achievable objectives. objectives for all the different types of alternative fuels, objectives closely linked to the priority ten-t network, on which we have worked a lot and which we have set ourselves as a reference point for the development of the infrastructure network. it is a directive which gives a clear direction to the market and which will enable car manufacturers, shipbuilders, energy producers and distributors and manufacturers of technical and technological components to have a certain framework in which to invest. with this work, we have broken the vicious circle that has characterized the alternative fuels sector until today. there is no infrastructure, and therefore there is no market. we have decided to break this vicious circle by starting with infrastructure investment, we call on the member states to take responsibility, but we are convinced that the burden on public investment will be relative because it will be possible, with a certain legislative framework, to involve the private sector in these investments. i would like to dedicate the last few seconds of my time to my shadow rapporteurs, with whom i have worked very fruitfully and whom i really thank for their spirit of cooperation.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report by mr fidanza on alternative fuels infrastructure, along the lines of the ppe. the report examines the commission's proposal to end oil dependence and accelerate the decarbonisation of the transport system by setting a set of minimum requirements for developing an alternative fuels infrastructure, including common technical specifications. this will also diversify and improve the security of the eu's energy supply. at the same time, the proposed directive should support economic growth, strengthen the competitiveness of european industry and reduce greenhouse gas emissions in the transport sector. i agree with the rapporteur in pointing out certain technological and commercial shortcomings which are somewhat slowing down the evolution of the alternative fuels market, including the lack of adequate infrastructure, the lack of common technical specifications necessary to ensure the interoperability and pan-european mobility of vehicles using alternative fuels. i welcome the amendments tabled by the rapporteur to supplement the provisions of the commission proposal and broaden its objectives with the ultimate aim of creating an effective strategy to attract private investment for infrastructure development, thus giving impetus to the use of alternative fuels.
in writing. - although the fidanza report is balanced and well thought out, i think it is still too early to want to force member states to invest in the electric car sector in terms of infrastructure, since there is still no scientific evidence to show that there are real benefits for industry and consumers in terms of both economic and transport facilitation, and for these reasons i have decided to abstain.
in writing. - i certainly support the report, which touches on a crucial point for the declared decarbonisation targets of the economy announced by the commission for 2030. while in many sectors, starting with energy, the share of fossils in the mix is clearly lagging behind, partly as a result of ambitious renewable energy programmes in the member states (think of the wind energy initiative announced by germany), on the mobility side, many developments have been hampered by insufficient infrastructure or by weak market penetration of technologies that are already widely available and have been in use for some time. just think of individual mobility or rubber logistics, which in many countries is significantly hampered by a weak or non-existent supply infrastructure. these inadequacies have a further impact on consumers in a market in some countries with major difficulties in the sale of new private or promiscuous vehicles, with obvious negative environmental, economic and productive repercussions. despite my philosophical preference for incentive mechanisms, the mandatory provision of minimum standards seems acceptable in the context of the directive, which leaves ample scope for member states to comply and transpose legislation according to individual specific situations.
in writing. - the main long-term objective should be the decarbonisation of the transport sector. i believe that action at union level is needed in addition to cost reductions, as the development of the alternative fuels market is still hampered by gaps and many market and technological shortcomings. a form of joint intervention would be necessary. i therefore expressly vote in favour.
in writing. - some european initiatives in the europe 2020 strategy aim to address major societal challenges such as climate change, energy and resource scarcity and to ensure more efficient use of energy. in line with that strategy, the commission proposal establishes a common framework of measures for the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure in the union, in order to break the oil dependency and accelerate the decarbonisation of the transport system. i voted in favour of the commission's proposal and i believe that action at union level is necessary, as the evolution of the alternative fuels market is still hampered by technological and commercial gaps, market failures, lack of consumer acceptance, lack of adequate infrastructure and, in many cases, lack of common technical specifications necessary to ensure the interoperability and pan-european mobility of vehicles using alternative fuels.
in writing. - the aim is to gradually replace oil with alternative fuels. there is currently little infrastructure for alternative fuels because there are few vehicles using them, and this leads to the production of vehicles at non-competitive prices and therefore consumers do not buy them. this vicious circle must be broken, and the first step is to build infrastructure. we must build the infrastructure by making minimum coverage mandatory by applying common techniques. for example, a minimum number of charging points for electric vehicles. in addition, consumers must be adequately informed. the directive, which is linked to the europe 2020 objectives, will therefore overcome this bottleneck without recourse to public spending, but through changes to local rules and proposals that promote private sector investment and eu support through ten-t, structural and cohesion funds.
in writing. - the transport system in the european union is still too dependent on oil as the main source of energy. alternative systems must be found if we are to succeed in diversifying the use of energy resources. the current commission proposal on alternative fuels infrastructure sets out a common framework of measures for the establishment of alternative fuels infrastructure in the union, a project which i agree with, particularly in view of the need to limit dependence on oil in the transport system. i therefore welcome the report by mr fidanza.
in writing. - the commission proposal is a necessary tool to end the eu's dependence on oil and to improve the diversification of its energy portfolio. this objective also makes it possible to pursue another objective at the same time, namely economic growth and the strengthening of the competitiveness of european industry, as well as the reduction of harmful emissions. it is therefore essential to adopt a coherent long-term strategy on alternative fuels, which preserves technological neutrality and meets the needs of all modes of transport. this strategy should naturally also have advantages in terms of innovation and inclusion. these objectives can be achieved by strengthening the supply infrastructure, which is still very limited in some sectors, and by a system which guarantees the quality of alternative fuels and includes a comprehensive, clear and comprehensive information system for consumers, so as to enable them to make informed choices.

in writing. - the directive aims to: (i) to improve the transparency and comparability of payment information relating to payment accounts, (ii) to facilitate switching between payment accounts, (iii) to eliminate discrimination based on residence in relation to payment accounts and (iv) to provide access to a payment account with basic features within the eu. the directive will apply to payment accounts held by consumers while accounts held by businesses are outside its scope. it doesn't cover the savings accounts.
in writing. - today parliament decided in plenary that anyone legally resident in the eu will have the right to open a basic bank account and no one will be denied this right on the basis of nationality or place of residence. i agree with the rapporteur, mr klute, that this directive, by guaranteeing access to basic accounts for all consumers, including migrants and mobile citizens, will stimulate economic modernisation and facilitate free movement. however, member states could require prospective customers to indicate their interest and the purpose of opening the account, provided that they fully respect the fundamental rights of the customer and that the exercise of that right is not excessively complicated or burdensome for the consumer. basic bank accounts allow customers to make payments or withdrawals and to carry out payment transactions within the eu, including payment card and online transactions. customers shall be allowed an unlimited number of such transactions at no cost or at a reasonable charge.
in writing. - following the ppe's position, i voted in favour of the report on the proposal for a regulation on key information documents (kids) for investment products, so that retail investors can make an appropriate investment decision. i welcome the work done so far by the european commission on the revision of eu legislation applicable to different types of retail investment products. this report focuses on the rules on product information in the context of packaged retail investment products (prip). the aim is to restore consumer confidence in financial markets, based on a thorough review of the insurance intermediation directive (imd), to ensure that consumers benefit from a high level of protection when buying insurance products and to strengthen the depositary function for ucits. the commission shall, by means of implementing acts, lay down the rules on the application of this article, in particular the rules on the application of article 4 (1) (a) of regulation (eu) no 648/2012 and the rules on the application of article 4 (1) (b) of regulation (eu) no 648/2012 to the provision of investment advice and sales services. i welcome the way the text is framed in terms of scope, taxation, risk indicators, information to investors on the use of funds, references to other regulations and the liability and sanctions regime.
in writing. - mr berès' report is well structured and acceptable. i consider it essential to enable retail investors to compare and better understand the main features and risks of the investment products they are about to put their savings into. for all these reasons i voted in favour of this text.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the new rules on the information which small investors, that is, non-professional investors, should receive before they sign a contract. under the new rules, all retail investors will be required to be given three pages of the key information document (kid) in a4 format before signing a contract. this will help retail investors to understand and compare insurance-based pre-packaged investment products (priips), estimate the total cost of their investment and be aware of the risk-return relationship.
in writing. - people who wish to invest their savings must be adequately informed of the characteristics (and risks) of such a decision. the information sheets are often unclear, difficult to read, and do not do their job as best as they can, which is to inform investors about a particular product. the new european regulation on this subject, on the other hand, lays down a few simple rules which should be observed: for example, the kid should be in a4 format, presented and structured in an easy-to-read manner, in legible typeface and in clear, concise and understandable language for the investors it is addressed to. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of the products is not compromised. if an individual is aware of this and has the right tools, then he can make the decisions he thinks are best to put his savings to good use.
in writing. - this regulation aims to ensure that investors are able to understand the main retail features and risks associated with investment products. at the same time, the regulation aims to ensure a level playing field between producers and sellers of these products. it therefore aims to establish uniform conditions at eu level. the proposal provides that the manufacturer of the investment product should draw up the key information document (kid) for each investment product it produces. manufacturers shall provide the kid to purchasers in good time before the conclusion of a transaction in the investment product. the new rules apply to all investment products for retail investors. however, they shall not apply to life and non-life insurance products, deposits other than structured deposits and securities and officially recognised pension schemes.
in writing. - although the commission has identified two areas for further development, namely the rules applicable to sales and the rules on product information, there are several points in european legislation which could be strengthened, starting from the scope, which is currently limited to pre-assembled investment products or investments with an indeterminate return. in addition, the indication of future performance scenarios based on a multi-factor analysis is to be preferred to risk indicators based on feedback on past performance. finally, the powers of the european supervisory authorities should be strengthened as regards liability and sanctions.

in writing. - since i believe that the appointment of judges to the court of justice, and therefore also that of the 12 additional judges, should remain the exclusive competence of the member states, i voted against this text.
in writing. - in recent years the number of cases pending has steadily increased, despite the enormous efforts made by the court, which is no longer able to cope with the increasing workload. the court of first instance nevertheless amended its rules of procedure to enable it to rule without an oral procedure on intellectual property cases, which can now be settled more quickly. it also decided to organise itself into eight different panels, alongside an appeals section. in order to further strengthen its capacity to deal with the cases brought before it, the court of justice proposed to increase the number of judges of the general court by 12 to 39, but raised the problem of designation. the latter could be solved by a rotation system allowing for an equal representation of the 28 countries in the court of justice, a subject which is very close to the hearts of the various national governments. but we must not forget the importance of the criterion of suitability, which the rapporteur brings to the attention of the house.

in writing. - i voted today in favour of the report on the introduction of an interoperable electronic emergency call service (ecall) throughout the european union. given the failure of the voluntary approach, the commission has started to adopt the necessary legislation to make ecall a mandatory service for new vehicles. parliament also contributed by approving in july 2012 by a large majority an own-initiative report entitled 'ecall: a new 112 service for citizens' to make it an eu-wide public emergency call system, installed on board vehicles, linked to the 112 emergency number and governed by common pan-european rules. the adoption of this report is a clear sign of parliament's desire to increase road safety. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the permissible sound power level of motor vehicles. this will inevitably mean faster response by emergency services, with the consequent reduction in the number of fatalities and the severity of injuries among drivers and european citizens.

member of the commission. - madam president, i would like to say thank you very much to everybody. i think that what we can say after the discussion is that basically we really all share the belief that something needs to be done. there are some things which i would like to clarify and i am pretty sure that you are aware of the majority of them. of course the idea of the proposal was not to address the whole issue of all plastic and the problems which are connected with plastic; that is something that we are working on separately and that is something which was not the real target of this proposal. the real target was to address one of the emblematic issues of our consumer society, and basically we all agree that this is an emblematic issue of our consumer society. so it is not a coincidence that we have practically unanimous public opinion support on this. we should use that public support, but not only use it; we have a responsibility to the public support we are receiving. the second thing i would like to mention is that, frankly, there was not a lot of lobbying of any kind from the business side when we discussed these proposals. predominantly, lightweight plastic bags are not produced in europe; they are imported from outside europe. that is the bare fact and is something you can find out from statistics, and i just want to say that i myself did not experience any kind of pressure from lobbying in this context. the third thing i would like to mention comes from the fact that many of you are talking about biodegradability as an answer. we are certainly not yet at the point where we could provide a definite answer; i can only say at this moment that when we have to deal with biodegradable plastic bags there are some questions which definitely need to be addressed. one is that biodegradable plastic too will only biodegrade within a reasonable time. so if we look at it from the point of view of marine litter, which was one of the core issues that we wanted to address, it does not provide an answer. secondly, mixing biodegradable and conventional plastics could – in fact would – disrupt composting and recycling operations. so that is also an issue that we need to bear in mind. so too is the broader picture when bio-based plastic is made from crops that are grown especially for production of plastic. this is not clear cut because there is quite a heavy burden on the environment too – land use, fertilisers, land treatment – so it is a life cycle approach which you have to look at. i am not saying that i am negative about this. i am just saying that these are open questions that will need to be addressed when talking about biodegradable plastics, and certainly these are issues which sooner or later we will need to address properly. finally, because many of you are also talking about the ambition of the proposal and especially in the context of potentially introducing a target, let me try to explain. i am a person who believes in targets so i think that targets normally work pretty well. we have been considering targets very seriously but currently we have a situation where two things are important and we cannot neglect them. we have huge differences amongst member states – there are countries which use more than 200 per person per year and countries which use only four per person per year, so what kind of target would work there – a relative one? an absolute one? what should be proposed? that is the first difficulty. the second difficulty is basically connected to the fact that in quite a number of member states there are different kinds of approaches which deliver results – which work! of course we have a target in mind. we believe something like a reduction of close to 80% can be achieved. that is why we have basically proposed tools which member states can use, including the one which goes as far as a ban – if this is in line with the treaty of course; it is a quite radical approach. we have proposed too an obligation on the member states that they prepare plans, targets and instruments, and use them. they will have to report to us, we will monitor this, and of course if we find that those proposals are not in line with something which one would believe would give results, then we still have the possibility to act in different ways. in concluding, maybe we do not need a heavyweight approach to the lightweight problems even if they do without any doubt place a heavy burden on our environment, but we need solutions and basically we all agree on that.
in writing. the report concerns the revision of directive 94/62, i.e. the reduction of the consumption of lightweight plastic bags. i welcome the compromise reached in the committee on the environment, public health and food safety - of which i am a full member - which gives member states adequate flexibility in choosing from a wide range of measures to reduce the consumption of plastic bags. the report says that member states will be free to decide whether to adopt economic instruments, such as taxation, or to maintain existing systems, including those involving the use of biodegradable and compostable bags. in particular, the report highlights the value of compostable biodegradable plastic bags made in accordance with the european standard, a material for which the italian industry is at the forefront at international level. member states will have the possibility to reduce the final cost of the bag where separate collection systems for organic waste are in place. i believe that the revision of the packaging and packaging waste directive, as it is designed, will give a new impetus to investment in the bio-economy, a sector in which italian industry boasts that it has been among the first and most innovative in europe.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it is absolutely essential to strengthen cooperation between the member states for operations coordinated by frontex, but this is the so-called trade union minimum, a policy on immigration and asylum which is still very far from being a common policy. to make this concept even clearer, i will give just a few figures: if the mediterranean flows continue as in the first months of 2014, italy will spend 110 million euros this year on border control and rescue operations. frontex has a total budget of eur 89 million, of which eur 34 million is allocated to administrative expenditure and the running of the agency alone. this means that, for 2014, frontex will only have 55 million available for operational activities, exactly half of what the italian government alone could spend. if we add to this the overall allocations of the immigration and asylum fund and the internal security fund, which are far lower than the commission's initial proposal, it is clear that there is a significant gap between what is declared and what is actually implemented at european level to ensure a genuine common immigration and asylum policy. for these reasons, i still believe that it is necessary to set up an operational headquarters for frontex in the mediterranean basin, perhaps in italy, by providing the agency with more resources and by limiting administrative costs as much as possible and, with the money thus saved, securing new agreements with the countries of origin and transit of migrants, also in order to combat trafficking in human beings.
